<reason>CON built and sustained a single decisive through-line — the dam hypothetical — and forced PRO to keep redrafting the "wanton" element until it collapsed into either a court weighing electricity against wetlands (arbitrary) or destruction with no benefit at all (largely redundant). PRO's pressure answer gave a concrete fact but effectively swapped the hypothetical rather than supplying a knowable standard for genuine trade-offs, and PRO's closing merely asserted the dilemma was "false." PRO did land real points: the redundancy horn is weakened because a domestic offense the complicit state refuses to prosecute doesn't supply a backstop, and the "should the complicit government have the last word" framing was clear. But PRO's positive mechanism shrank to an executive being careless enough to fly into a member state, and CON's two-tier/capital-avoidance cost was never squarely answered. CON's execution was imperfect — two clipped turns and a bogus reference ID ([P1.3, P2.3]) — which narrows the margin, but CON made the debate easier to decide and did more damage to the opponent's live route.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A4.2–A4.3: after PRO's A1 replaced "clearly excessive" balancing with an equally cheap alternative rejected "without any material public benefit," CON's dilemma that the balancing element either does real work and is arbitrary, or does none and the crime is redundant — PRO's closing answered redundancy reasonably but never supplied the standard for the arbitrariness horn.</best_rebuttal>
